content.title: 16 FOOD FACTS THAT SOUND MADE UP BUT ARE 100% REAL
facts: **Nutmeg** – in large enough doses it acts as a hallucinogen; just a couple teaspoons can cause hours of hallucinations and sickness.
**Apples** – they float because about 25% of their volume is air, which is also why they're buoyant in water.
**Carrots** – they were originally purple; the orange variety was bred in the Netherlands around the 17th century.
**Strawberries** – they aren't technically berries, but bananas and avocados are, botanically speaking.
**Peanuts** – they're not nuts at all, they're legumes that grow underground, related to peas and lentils.
**Cashews** – the raw version sold in stores doesn't exist in nature; truly raw cashews contain a toxin related to poison ivy's and must be steamed first.
**Pineapples** – the enzyme bromelain in fresh pineapple actually breaks down proteins, which is why your tongue can feel raw after eating a lot of it.
**Rice** – a single grain of wild rice can take over a year to fully mature and harvest by hand in traditional paddies.
**Chili peppers** – capsaicin, the compound that makes them hot, doesn't actually burn tissue; it just tricks your heat receptors into firing.
**Watermelon** – it's about 92% water, which is close enough to drinking water that it was historically used to hydrate travelers in dry regions.
**Saffron** – it takes around 75,000 crocus flowers, hand-picked, to produce just one pound of saffron threads.
**Follow along** – for more daily food facts that sound fake but are completely true.
content.caption:
Quick mind-benders worth knowing: cashews sold raw in stores aren't actually raw — true raw cashews carry a toxin similar to what's in poison ivy, so every batch gets steamed or roasted before it ever reaches a shelf, which is why 'raw cashews' at the store are a bit of a misnomer. Pineapple's bite isn't just acidity — the enzyme bromelain is a protein-digesting compound so active it's used industrially to tenderize meat, and your mouth literally starts to feel it breaking down your tongue's surface proteins. And chili peppers never actually burn you — capsaicin binds to the same receptors that detect real heat, so your brain reacts as if you touched a flame even though no tissue damage occurs. Food chemistry is wild, and everyone's tolerance for these reactions is a little different.
